node.label: Kathy Peiss
node.date_label: Cheap Amusements (1986) · Hope in a Jar (1998) · Zoot Suit (2011) · Information Hunters (online 2019; print 2020)
node.description: In Cheap Amusements (1986), Kathy Peiss argued that young working women’s leisure and sexual expressiveness helped create commercial mass culture in turn-of-the-century New York. Hope in a Jar (1998) showed how women as beauty entrepreneurs and users of cosmetics helped build American beauty culture, combining opportunities for self-definition with new constraints. Marybeth Hamilton praised Cheap Amusements as a contribution to women’s labour history but criticized its romanticizing tone and insufficient engagement with reformers’ objections to commercial leisure. In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss used gender analysis to question histories that treated business as naturally masculine and women chiefly as workers or consumers. Her later historiographical essay, Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), assessed the gains and limits of the gender turn, questioning inconsistent definitions of gender and recurring explanations based on masculine crisis.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Cheap Amusements: Working Women and Leisure in Turn-of-the-Century New York (1986); Passion and Power: Sexuality in History (1989), coedited with Christina Simmons; Hope in a Jar: The Making of America’s Beauty Culture (1998); “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures: Conceptualizing Gender in Twentieth Century Business History (1998); Zoot Suit: The Enigmatic Career of an Extreme Style (2011); Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013); Information Hunters: When Librarians, Soldiers, and Spies Banded Together in World War II Europe (online 2019; print 2020).
node.scope_note: The 2013 chapter, pp. 17–37 including notes, was read through NYU Press’s authorized open-access PDF. Selected passages of the 1998 Business History Review article were read, especially pp. 219–223 and 231–237; the 1998 consumer-culture lecture was read in its journal transcription. Hamilton’s review was read at pp. 283–285. Cheap Amusements, Hope in a Jar, Zoot Suit and Information Hunters were not read in full; their selected publication facts and broader descriptions come from institutional and publisher records. Scott’s 1998 response was available only as an extract and through Scranton’s account; the Bederman, Kessler-Harris and Hoganson originals discussed in the proposed links remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss uses the gender-analysis framework associated with Scott’s Gender and the Politics of History (1988) to explain how business practices represent and produce economic power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed pp. 221–222, especially the paragraph beginning “The framework for gender analysis pioneered by Joan Scott”; notes 4–5 identify Scott’s 1988 book alongside other feminist resources. This is a specific methodological use and recommendation, not sole derivation or a claim of supervision. Scott’s book was not independently read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss uses Bederman’s Manliness and Civilization (1995) to treat masculinity as a continuing historical process rather than assume a singular crisis of manhood.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed p. 222, paragraph beginning “This approach is especially powerful,” calls masculinity an “always problematic category” following Bederman; note 6 identifies the 1995 book. The use concerns business organization and gender; no wholesale adoption of Bederman’s book or fresh reading of that original is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), Peiss questions the shifting definitions of gender in Kessler-Harris’s Do We Still Need Women’s History? (2007), using it to illustrate inconsistent applications of gender analysis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed p. 31, paragraph beginning “Nevertheless,” and note 34 (p. 37), referring back to the full citation in note 30: Chronicle of Higher Education, 7 December 2007, B6–7. Peiss introduces the example as “flattened and inconsistent concepts of gender.” On p. 30 she also acknowledges Kessler-Harris’s concern that women’s history remains unfinished; the critique is not a rejection of that concern. Kessler-Harris’s original was not read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), Peiss includes Hoganson’s Fighting for American Manhood (1998) in a qualified criticism of histories whose recurring masculine-crisis explanations risk essentializing masculinity across different settings.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed pp. 31–32, especially the paragraph beginning “Boydston’s observations hold true,” with note 36 on p. 37 explicitly naming Hoganson alongside Summers, Dean and Gosse. The phrase “markedly similar, if not uniform” describes the cluster, not Hoganson alone. Peiss separately values Consumers’ Imperium (2007) at p. 28/note 25. The link is a bounded collective criticism, not a blanket dismissal of Hoganson; both Hoganson books remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), Peiss connects women’s history’s feminist and institutional formation with the continuing task of integrating women’s actions into wider historical explanations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter pp. 17–20 and 30–33: the opening identifies four conceptual turns; the conclusion assesses progress “from exclusion to inclusion.” Pages 32–33 retain women’s agency as a continuing concern alongside gender analysis. Complete chapter and notes read in the authorized NYU PDF; no claim that gender history supersedes women’s history.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women’s history and its institutional formation

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss asks how business helped construct gender as well as how gender shaped business, questioning the treatment of firms as naturally masculine.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Article pp. 219–223, especially pp. 220–221 on the firm as a “masculine enterprise” and the paired questions about gender’s operation in business and business’s construction of gender. The reading includes the opening argument and named methodological resources, not the entire article.
proposed_edges.map_label: Business and gender shape one another

proposed_edges.relationship: In American Women and the Making of Modern Consumer Culture (1998), Peiss argues that women helped produce consumer culture through commercial work, political organizing and beauty businesses as well as purchasing goods.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Journal transcription, opening paragraphs on the historical production of consumer identity and final paragraphs on African American beauty entrepreneurs and collective alternatives; conclusion beginning “Behind the compelling image.” The lecture was delivered 26 March 1998 and published in the Fall 1998 journal issue. Read as an argument, not inferred from a shared topic or a teaching appointment.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women as makers of consumer culture

proposed_edges.relationship: Cheap Amusements (1986) connects women’s wage work and leisure to cultural change, a contribution to women’s labour history identified by Marybeth Hamilton’s review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hamilton’s review, pp. 283–285, opens by identifying “women’s labour history” and explains the connection between work schedules, low wages and recreation. The book itself remains unread in full; this field link is explicitly mediated by the named reviewer.
proposed_edges.map_label: Working women’s leisure and cultural change

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Bad Girls and Masked Men” (1997), Carolyn Strange draws on Kathy Peiss’s Cheap Amusements (1986), alongside Erenberg and Nasaw, to explain the shift toward mixed-sex commercial leisure, and uses Peiss’s evidence on working women’s family circumstances in her comparison of sexual opportunities and constraints.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Journal PDF passages read. The body attributes the leisure transition to Peiss, Erenberg and Nasaw jointly; notes 9–10 connect the subsequent analysis to Cheap Amusements, pp. 34 and 52. This is documented use in Strange’s essay, not a claim of exclusive influence or supervision. Peiss’s book was not read in full.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses leisure history to compare sexual opportunities

proposed_edges.relationship: Cheap Amusements (1986) contributes to the history of sexuality by showing how commercial leisure gave working-class women sexual autonomy alongside new vulnerabilities and dependencies, an insight Regina Kunzel uses in “The Uneven History of Modern American Sexuality” (2018) to historicize heterosexuality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher HTML body and notes read. Kunzel explicitly uses Peiss to address the historical construction of heterosexuality. The field endpoint includes sexuality history; this does not assert that Peiss studied gay identities. Kunzel is not an eligible person endpoint, so no person edge is proposed.
